idiom_name: transactional handle plus read-set / write-set commit
implementation_notes: There is no generic implementation - the pattern is a structure that must be built, and the decision is which of four components you implement. You need (1) a transactional handle: a mutable cell whose target may only be replaced inside a transaction; (2) a version counter or immutable node identity attached to every value, so 'did this change' is answerable without locking; (3) a transaction context holding a read set of (handle, observed value) and a write set of deferred replacements; and (4) a commit that validates every read-set entry against current state and publishes the write set atomically, with abort simply discarding both sets. If (2) can be an immutable structure's root pointer, use that - then 'changed' is pointer inequality and the undo is keeping the old pointer, which is far cheaper than copying values. Keep (1)-(4) in one module rather than distributing them, because the discipline that must be auditable is: every mutable shared value goes through a handle, and nothing outside commit touches the underlying storage. The transaction body must be a pure function of the handles it touches; that is what makes re-execution safe. The generic form is worth building once per process and reusing, because the alternative - every team hand-writing a CAS-and-retry loop - produces subtly different and differently-broken versions of the same pattern.
code_sketch:
transaction(body):
    readset = [];  writeset = []
    repeat:
        committed = false
        try:
            for h in readset: h.revert_to(observed)   # undo, in LIFO
            readset.clear(); writeset.clear()
            body(readset, writeset)                    # MUST be side-effect free
            for (h, observed) in readset:
                if h.current is not observed: raise Conflict
            for (h, value) in writeset: h.install(value)
            committed = true
        except Conflict:
            continue                                    # whole block re-runs
    return result
pitfalls: Installing writes one location at a time breaks atomicity: another thread can observe a partially-applied transaction between two installs. Commit must publish all writes as one step (immutable root swap, or a lock-free multi-word CAS).
Recording the read set after the read rather than before lets a concurrent change slip between the read and the record.
Forgetting the in-transaction value: a transaction that reads a value it has already written must see its own write, not the snapshot.
Unbounded history: keeping every old version so slow transactions can still be served is correct but unbounded; cap it and accept that very old transactions must retry.
Implementing abort as compensation logic rather than as discarding the sets - compensation is the anti-pattern the pattern exists to remove.
